items.title: I want my Wednesday back
items.content:
Or, why we’re not seeing mass-exploitation of php2shell yet.

I saw wildly varying opinions on whether php2shell is serious, or if they cried wolf. Got curious, started digging into the PoCs. I’m not an exploit dev and maybe there were other factors, so take with a grain of salt. Egg on my face if mass exploitation starts right as I hit publish.

Best PoC of php2shell I’ve found: https://github.com/9bie/php2shell-bypass-aslr-exp (and a fork with all docs translated to english )

To exploit, you need to do four consecutive requests to the same php worker process . And you need to know the exact php build (php version, OS version, architecture), or try exploits for every possible build.

What this PoC does is take a docker image that uses the default mod_php number of workers, which is 150. Then it opens 149 connections that send half a request to keep the other workers busy, and does the four exploit requests against the 150th worker.

Even a moderately popular production website will have multiple web VMs/containers running multiple php workers behind a load balancer and constant bot traffic. That means you would have to try a wide range of number of connections to open. On top of that you likely won’t know the exact build version, so you would have to try exploits for every combination out there.

Let’s say you try this for the 50 most popular php/OS combinations, and any number of workers between 10 and 1010. That’s 50k attempts. But against constant background traffic, you would need to try each combination a number of times. Each of these attempts involves opening a whole lot of connections, so they each take some time. The PoC runs against localhost and takes 3-4 seconds, so let’s optimistically call it 10 seconds on the internet.

You can only do one attempt at a time, so that means multiple days of bruteforcing in a way that is essentially a DoS, since a large part of that range will exhaust the maximum number of connections. At this point the person running the site will likely notice, start blocking IP addresses or adding a WAF.

Most high-traffic websites already run WAFs/rate-limiting to deal with bot traffic, so you would need to run this attack from a great many IPs, and preferably clean ones that are harder to come by. But running this from many IPs also increases the chances that your timing will be off, reducing the number of plausible attempts even further.

That’s assuming the WAF doesn’t block your attempts entirely, because the easiest ways to exploit these vulnerabilities were known at the time of the announcement.

I’m sure people and agents will come up with clever techniques to reduce the required number of attempts eventually. But that has nothing to do with “this will get mass-exploited within 15 minutes.”

Against very low-traffic websites that do not have any bot protection, leak information about their version, running close to stock configuration, you might get lucky.

So sure, it’s a critical vulnerability, deserves attention, should be patched ASAP. Maybe even put in the announcement that if you’re running low-traffic sites, be extra sure to patch fast.

But to the AI security vendors who promoted this as THE GATES OF HELL WILL OPEN YOU HAVE TO PATCH WITHIN 15 MINUTES OR DIE? I want my Wednesday back.

Oh and the claims of it being exploited in the wild? At time of writing, they’re referring to exploitation attempts . In fact, HoneyLabs so far hasn’t seen a single exploit attempt that could even run successfully.

items.title: AI bubble update: 79% of companies say their GPUs sit idle at least half the time, yet most plan new AI platforms
items.content:
Most surveyed companies running AI in production say the GPUs they use sit idle at least half the time, and most of those companies plan to add or switch AI compute platforms anyway, according to the latest data from VentureBeat Intelligence.

A whopping 79% of the 218 respondents who reported GPU utilization said their GPUs are busy half the time or less, across three monthly VB Pulse surveys from July through September . Among those companies, 70% said they plan to adopt a new, additional or replacement AI compute platform within the next 12 months. The share with idle GPUs held between 77% and 81% in each of the three months. We reported the September results Thursday ; the three months of data show the pattern holding steady.

Those numbers matter because Wall Street is arguing over whether AI is a bubble. On October 13, the International Monetary Fund warned that a sharp fall in AI share prices could threaten global financial stability . Most of that argument has focused on the companies selling AI compute, such as Nvidia, cloud giants Microsoft, Google and Amazon Web Services, and specialized GPU clouds like CoreWeave, and on whether they are building more capacity than their customers will pay for. We looked at what those customers are actually doing.

At first glance, the numbers look like a contradiction. Why would companies with so much unused GPU capacity plan to add or switch AI compute platforms? And why would they leave GPUs idle when, as technology leaders tell me, they are under heavy pressure in this fall's budget season to cut their AI bills?

The demand for AI is real, but it is landing in a different place than the idle GPUs. Professionals and consumers keep using more AI, and much of that work runs through the frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI. That demand will keep supporting those companies' spending on compute for some time. The mismatch sits one level down, inside enterprises that are paying for two kinds of AI that cannot easily stand in for each other.

The first kind is capacity. I believe many companies were scared by reports of GPU shortages in 2024 and 2025 and lined up GPU capacity so they would not be caught short. Much of the capacity companies use sits idle, our surveys show, though the surveys did not ask how companies got that capacity or whether they controlled it directly..

The second kind is frontier models. Engineers and other employees have preferred the most capable models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, paid by the token through those companies' APIs, through monthly subscriptions or through the big cloud providers. The thinking was that companies needed the best intelligence to race ahead, and they would sort out the economics later. Uber's chief technology officer, Praveen Neppalli Naga, said in August that "we're coming to the end of the so-called tokenmaxxing era," after Uber spent its 2026 AI budget within a few months, according to Fortune. An AI leader at a Fortune 500 company, speaking on background, told me in October that AI costs keep rising, and that while the company expects productivity gains to offset them eventually, it does not know that yet.

Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Google now sell Anthropic's or OpenAI's models through their clouds, and OpenAI said on Wednesday that its models will reach Google Cloud in the coming weeks. OpenAI's frontier GPT models and Anthropic's Claude models are closed, so the cloud provider or the model maker runs them on its own infrastructure and bills by the token or for capacity reserved for that one model. A company cannot load them onto GPUs it already controls. To shift work onto those GPUs, a company has to switch to an open-weight model and run it itself. items.summary_ko: VentureBeat Intelligence의 최신 조사에 따르면, 프로덕션에서 AI를 운영하는 기업 대다수가 GPU를 최소 절반 이상 유휴 상태로 두고 있다. GPU 활용률을 응답한 218개 기업 중 79%가 가동 시간이 절반 이하라고 답했고, 이 중 70%는 향후 12개월 안에 새로운, 추가 또는 교체용 AI 컴퓨팅 플랫폼을 도입할 계획이라고 밝혔다. 이 비율은 3개월 조사 내내 77~81% 범위를 유지했다.
items.content_ko: 조사 대상 기업 대다수가 GPU를 절반 이상 쉬게 두고 있지만, 그럼에도 많은 기업이 AI 컴퓨팅 플랫폼을 추가하거나 바꿀 계획이라고 한다. 7월부터 9월까지 세 차례 진행된 VB Pulse 설문 결과가 근거다. 이 수치는 월가에서 AI가 거품인지를 두고 벌어지는 논쟁과 맞닿아 있다. 매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

items.content:

Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech. Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493, see the first chart below. Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493, see the second chart below. And there are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth, see the third chart below. With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins.

VC-backed companies are spending more and more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it. As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited, see the fourth and fifth charts below.

The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins. That may be harder than it sounds. AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment. Judgment depends on context, and the answer varies with which human or which model you ask. Perhaps most importantly, AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.

The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector.

items.title: Balloting has completed for C++26. Unfortunately it was Disapproved
items.content:
P-Members voting: 12 in favor out of 20 = 60 % (requirement >= 66.66%)

(P-Members having abstained are not counted in this vote.)

Member bodies voting: 9 negative votes out of 22 = 41 % (requirement <= 25%)

Sort of a sad day for the C++ community. Hopefully we can heal and move on from this in a productive manner.

There were 12 countries that abstained. In several cases because they could not reach to a common position. That is another signal of a contested draft.

Please, note that before C++26 all other standards passed unanimously.

Why should this be a sad day for the C++ community? Taking into account the number of P-members who abstained due to a lack of consensus, which makes the NO vote even more significant, sinking such a flawed contracts proposal is a good sign of a healthy, engaged, and competent community at the national body level.

That some people were willing to put the entire C++26 standard at risk to push through such a controversial and deeply flawed proposal is, of course, concerning. Fortunately, the national bodies recognized the problem before it was too late.

And perhaps it is also a clear signal that WG21's 'experts in the room' voting approach needs to be reconsidered.

I assume this was not a complete surprise and that those who voted against it had voiced opposition or at least reservations previously? Is the most promising path forward to reduce the scope and try again? Or were there things excluded that people really wanted?

Such is the life of standards. Anything particular?

It is hard to heal after the decades of the same social issues reappearing. What lessons should we learn to be able to move on in a productive manner?

12 in favor out of 20 who did not abstain gets 8 voting against, but then we have 9 negative votes out of 22? Not that it matters terribly since it doesn't seem very close.

So sad to hear this, but indeed, let's learn from this, and regroup and move on.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Twelve years of distributed SQLite
items.content:
In September 2014 I published a short post announcing rqlite . The idea was simple: take SQLite , put a Raft log in front of it, and replicate every write to a cluster so that the loss of a node did not mean the loss of the data. The source went on GitHub that same weekend. As far as I can tell, that was the first open-source system to combine Raft and SQLite. Nobody else was doing it, and for several years nobody else tried.

Today “distributed SQLite” is a category with a dozen projects in it, a few of them venture-funded, two of them acquired. Since the people now writing about the category tend to start the story around 2021, I thought I should write down the version that starts in 2014. I was there for all of it.

The need was concrete. A clustered system I worked on at jut.io needed a small amount of relational storage, and the question of which node should hold it had no good answer. Replicating SQLite with a consensus protocol solved it. We went another way at work, but I kept building rqlite because the problem was general and the solution was small. The first version used goraft , the same library InfluxDB  and etcd used at the time (I subsequently joined InfluxDB as a core developer around the same time). In early 2016 I replaced it with Hashicorp’s Raft implementation which rqlite still uses.

The design decision that mattered most was made then and never changed. rqlite is a CP system . Writes must go through the leader, a majority must acknowledge, and a partitioned minority refuses writes. Everything else, the HTTP API , the read-consistency levels , the snapshotting , followed from that.

Two things deserve mention for honesty’s sake. Expensify had been replicating SQLite inside its own infrastructure for years with a Paxos -style protocol; they released it as Bedrock in 2016 . And ActorDB, an Erlang system that gave each “actor” its own SQLite database replicated by Raft, appeared around the same time as rqlite . Neither was widely adopted outside its origin, but both show the idea was in the air. What rqlite did was make it a standalone, general-purpose, open-source thing anyone could run.

Canonical built dqlite to get LXD and later MicroK8s an embedded replicated store without running etcd. Mark Shuttleworth actually called me once, and we talked, hoping that rqlite could be made to work, but it never quite fit. dqlite began in Go and was rewritten in C with its own Raft library. It is the project most similar to rqlite in intent, and the main difference is of one of packaging: dqlite is a library you embed, rqlite is a server you run. Canonical’s need was a database inside their products: mine was a database beside anyone’s product.

2021: Litestream, and a change of approach

Ben Johnson (whom I worked with at InfluxDB) released Litestream in early 2021 . Litestream does not use consensus at all. It watches the SQLite WAL and streams it to S3 , giving you disaster recovery for a single-node SQLite database at almost no cost. Ben’s argument was that most applications do not need a cluster; they use one machine and need a way to recover if it dies. He was right about a great many applications, and the “SQLite is enough” movement of the next few years, with blog posts and conference talks, owes a lot to that argument.

Litestream and rqlite answer different questions. Litestream: what if the machine dies? rqlite: what if the machine dies and I cannot wait to restore? The first question is more common, the second is the one people have when they come to rqlite.

Fly.io hired Ben in 2022 and shipped LiteFS , which replicates SQLite at filesystem level with leases from Consul . It was the first attempt to make replicated SQLite a platform feature rather than a thing you deploy. And in a final twist, Litestream inspired rqlite’s v8.0 approach to handling the SQLite WAL.

SQLite를 합의 프로토콜로 복제하면 이 문제를 풀 수 있었고, 저자는 회사에서는 다른 방식을 택했지만 문제가 일반적이고 해법이 작다는 이유로 rqlite 개발을 이어갔다. 첫 버전은 InfluxDB와 etcd가 당시 쓰던 goraft 라이브러리를 사용했다. 글 작성자는 이후 InfluxDB에 합류했다고 밝힌다. 이 글은 오늘날 많은 사람이 2021년부터 이야기를 시작하는 분산 SQLite의 역사를 2014년부터 기록하려는 시도다.

items.title: Indian government sites are serving revoked eMudhra certificates
items.content:
On 17th October, eight eMudhra intermediate CAs chaining to emSign ECC Root CA - G3 were found to have trivially recoverable private keys . They were revoked the next day, and Mozilla and Chrome are now distrusting the G3 root. Separately, on 19th October eMudhra revoked 9,356 certificates on its unaffected RSA hierarchy (emSign Root CA - G1) with the reason “Superseded”. That batch matches every unexpired certificate missing a certificate-type policy OID required by emSign’s own CP/CPS ( Bug 2082782 ).

On 21st October, MeitY posted this thread :

A security incident concerning eMudhra’s Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) was reported in the public domain. […]

However, some social media accounts are indulging in fear mongering about the impact of this incident. […]

The impact of this incident on Indian websites and applications have been very limited and for a very short interval.

— @GoI_MeitY , 21st October 2026, 16:31 CEST

That last claim is wrong on both counts. The interval wasn’t short: the flawed keys were generated in April 2025, so anyone could have recovered them for 18 months before the report. The impact isn’t limited either: the compromised intermediates barely issued anything, but Mozilla and Chrome are now distrusting the entire G3 root, so eMudhra estimates 30,000 certificates from its unaffected G3 intermediates must be migrated. From what I could see, most of those seem to belong to US universities using eMudhra through InCommon rather than Indian sites.

Meanwhile, the 19th October revocations have left Indian government sites serving revoked certificates days later , including four bodies under MeitY itself: STPI , Bhashini , UIDAI , and the Controller of Certifying Authorities, whose India PKI site is serving a revoked eMudhra certificate. Notably, Controller of Certifying Authorities regulates eMudhra’s CA business in India.

I checked the 8,947 hosts in the IGOD directory of Indian government websites. As of 23rd October, 156 of them are still serving one of these revoked certificates. All of them were revoked between 15:34 and 15:49 CEST on 19th October, and are listed in eMudhra’s CRLs for DV/G2A-1 , OV/G2A-1 , EV/G2A-1 and G1 .

Whether these sites open depends on your browser. Firefox ships CRLite , which covers every revocation, and refuses to load them. Chrome’s CRLSet (version 10856, 24th October) has none of these certificates, nor any of the 6,235 entries on the DV/G2A-1 CRL, so Chrome, Edge and Android load them fine. So does Safari on iOS, which only checks OCSP for EV certificates. Two sites on the list have one: www.isea.gov.in and nfscnagpur.nic.in , and emSign’s OCSP responder reports the isea.gov.in certificate as revoked, so Safari on iOS refuses to load it. SSL Labs checks the CRL itself and marks all of these as Grade F / revoked.

Revocations happen (GoDaddy just revoked 4 lakh certificates), but they are usually accompanied by notifications to subscribers to

get them to new valid certificates. I’m not sure if eMudhra is doing any of the sort, now that they don’t care about their TLS business.

The table will be updated with timestamps as cert rotations happen.

items.title: ‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentre
items.content:
Finnish forest cleared for data centre development

‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentre

Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push

Behind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google’s arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees occupied the 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest near the town of Muhos in rural northern Finland . Now they are all gone.

After the tech company illegally stripped the entire area to build a datacentre – taking even the top soil with it – all that remains is a vast expanse of mud indented with the trail marks of machinery, puddles and mounds of earth, roots and branches. Residents say that brown water flowing off the site is going into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River.

“It doesn’t end. It goes on and on,” says Mari Annala, an ecologist from the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation (SLL), looking at drone footage of the former forest from the perimeter.

Mari Annala is a Finnish environmental expert, researcher and board member of the Oulu region district of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation. Photograph: Jarno Artika/The Guardian With 145 new datacentres at various stages of planning, Finland has found itself at the forefront of the tech companies’ latest push. As well as its relative geopolitical and geological stability and abundance of land, the cool climate makes it especially attractive for saving on energy costs.

Map Earlier this month, Google was ordered by the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) to temporarily stop work on Muhos and another site about 100km south-east in the village of Otanmäki after it failed to complete the necessary environmental impact assessments before clearcutting the land. The news has prompted widespread outcry and a national reckoning over what role, if any, the country should play in the global rush to build datacentres to keep up with rapid AI development.

Last week, Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, apologised for the forest clearings but claimed the company had acted “on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time”.

In the northern Finnish town of Muhos, the forest has already been cut down on land acquired by Google, with excavators now clearing the ground and rumbling trucks shuttling back and forth to the construction area located next to major power lines. Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen

An aerial view of the site where Google’s data centre was set to be built in Muhos. Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty Images Muhos and Otanmäki are part of a €13bn AI infrastructure project by Google that has attracted criticism from Donald Trump, who would rather the centres were built in the US and has publicly called for the company to reconsider. It is the biggest ever project of its kind in the Nordic country.

The Finnish government, which has presided over deep spending cuts, has encouraged the investment. Last month, when the Google plans were announced, the country’s prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said attracting investment was a “top priority” and “the value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment”. He said the Google deal would “deliver lasting benefits for both parties”.

But the revelations over Google’s misconduct have prompted public concern over what these deals mean for nearby communities, energy prices for Finnish households and Finland’s natural environment, a national source of pride. The datacentre push is likely to become a key election issue when Finns go to the polls in April.

Google’s clearcut area is 3km long and 2km wide, 330 hectares in total, and 400 metres from the Oulujoki River. Photograph: Jarno Artika/The Guardian In addition to the 250,000 trees felled at Muhos, Annala estimates that an additional 150,000 trees were felled at…

items.title: Barney: A Progress Update
items.content:
Hello all and welcome to the new blog! I'm Ikey Doherty and a little while back, I declared war on the industry .

Unfortunately during that time many have cherry-picked singular data points and have failed to grasp the entire picture so

The barney project is under active development and I expect many parts to

change in time. While the DSL is well considered, the exact syntax and nature

As a software engineer of course it triggers me somewhat when I see techbros going all-in AI-slop on a respin and selling it as

the elixer of life. And of course, insult to injury, at the time of my announcement Omarchy was being backed left right and center

That in itself wasn't entirely interesting. Instead, the absolute racist drivel being shoved into the limelight by DHH regarding nomadic

people, his comments on how to "deal" with gypsies, pissed me off. I'm an Irish Traveller, and I find any such rhetoric about nomadic

people utterly disgusting. No, I'm not talking about "digital nomads" I'm talking about people much like me that have been oppressed

and persecuted for hundreds of years, indigenous nomadic people.

See the big picture here a minute. When someone like DHH with his vile views, becomes the de-facto posterboy of the software industry...

we're in big shit. The industry at large is happily backing his ventures and normalising his views, which to me is an existential threat.

Hence Barney. Not so much as "no AI slop" but "here's something built by someone you clearly despise due to their background outdoing you

without requiring a right-wing techbro circle of investers". Simply put: defiance in the face of a woefully corrupted industy.

Or just pure old school "fuck you" vibes. Take your pick.

OK, enough with the war cries, let's have a look at the foundation of Barney: A proper DSL. Not completely NIH - don't worry. It's

based on KDL . Essentially I'm building a compiler approach that's building an AST atop the core KDL pass.

Core to the whole design is the central distro file. Essentially this contains the main phases of the bootstrap/build, setting specific variables

for each phase run. Incidentally the currently building phase will be exported as phase for binding/reuse in other modules and recipes.

Instead of allowing arbitrary shell scripts or string substitutions I've insisted on a hashable, verifiable chain of custody. Effectively we have

a mini scripting language in the DSL in execute sections of modules. Quite simply a script bakes to a list of enums, which can be of the following

Internally we will bind an absolute minimum number of functions, ie emit . The entire purpose of a script is to reliably generate a shell-compatible

script in a reproducible fashion. Essentially it's a string builder with a functional approach, without requiring complex semantics. For some ease of

use we will adopt Rust-style namespace resolution, i.e. autotools::configure .

emit (prop)command " --prefix= " (prop)prefix

Right now I haven't implemented the recipe format itself as it's genuinely the least interesting element right now.

The semantics come from the modules, the logic or "magic" is from the design and there will be no special features in

the DSL that need to be implemented for the recipe itself.

It's worth pointing out that flavours / profiles / etc are to be baked into the hashes throughout the entire chain.

You may be wondering, hold on, how do I do complex scripting in the recipes? By and large we'll avoid it because those

unavoidable, it will be checked in as some script or patch file to ensure it is hashed and doesn't accidentally blow

온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: UK police detective faces a gross misconduct probe for using Microsoft Copilot to assess risk and justify decisions in criminal cases. The watchdog says the officer also fed it sensitive case data.
items.content:
IOPC investigating officer’s use of AI in criminal investigations

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) is investigating allegations a detective used artificial intelligence (AI) inappropriately during criminal investigations.

Derbyshire Constabulary made a voluntary conduct referral to us on 23 June following an internal review of the officer’s AI use and concerns it may not have been in line with guidance and conditions issued by the force.

It’s alleged the officer used AI to create policy decisions, assess and manage risk, and to justify decision making, and that sensitive operational and personal data relating to cases was also inputted.

We assessed the detail contained in the referral and decided the matter required investigation and that it was right for us to carry out the investigation independently.

The officer has been served notice advising they are being investigated for alleged gross misconduct.

IOPC Director of Engagement, Emily Barry, said: “These are serious allegations and it’s right they are investigated thoroughly and independently.

“We understand Derbyshire Constabulary authorised the use of Microsoft Copilot for officers in May 2025 with guidance on how it could be used to aid productivity in drafting reports and summarising information. There were conditions on its use, including that no operational, sensitive or personal data should be inputted to AI.

“Our investigation will analyse the officer’s use of Copilot between May last year and June this year and assess if there are any potential breaches of police professional standards.”

items.title: Raku Course updates – Andrew Shitov
items.content:
My Complete Course of the Raku programming language got a few useful updates.

First, it now covers all the three Raku compilers (Rakudo, Raku++, and mutsu) and gives instructions on how to install and use them.

Second, the Course got it’s own mobile application with the whole content and a built-in Raku++ compiler. The users can run most of the examples directly on the app pages as well as run their own programs in the built-in playground. The playground is a full Raku++ compiler port for the mobile devices, both iOS and Android, and also can run code, which the browser WASM version cannot.

And third, the course pages are now equipped with the Run button, so you can directly run the code and see the result. The snippets are editable, so you can change the code to learn deeper. This applies to all the translations. Look at how the Run button works on a random page , for example.

As before, feedback is welcome as issues in the GitHub repositories:

items.summary_ko: Raku 강좌에 세 가지 업데이트가 적용되었다. 세 가지 Raku 컴파일러(Rakudo, Raku++, mutsu)의 설치와 사용법을 다루며, 내장 Raku++ 컴파일러를 탑재한 모바일 앱이 출시되었다. 강좌 페이지에는 코드를 바로 실행할 수 있는 Run 버튼이 추가되었고, 이는 모든 번역본에 적용된다.
items.content_ko: Andrew Shitov의 Raku 강좌에 세 가지 개선이 이루어졌다. 첫째, 강좌가 Rakudo, Raku++, mutsu 세 가지 컴파일러를 모두 다루며 각각의 설치와 사용법을 안내한다. 둘째, 전체 내용을 담은 전용 모바일 앱이 나왔고 Raku++ 컴파일러가 내장되어 있다. 예제 대부분을 앱 페이지에서 바로 실행할 수 있으며, 자신의 프로그램을 내장 플레이그라운드에서 돌려볼 수도 있다. 이 플레이그라운드는 모바일용 Raku++ 컴파일러로, iOS와 Android에서 모두 동작하며 브라우저의 WASM 버전으로는 실행할 수 없는 코드도 실행할 수 있다. 셋째, 강좌 페이지에 Run 버튼이 추가되어 코드를 바로 실행하고 결과를 확인할 수 있다. 스니펫은 편집할 수 있어 코드를 바꿔 보며 더 깊이 배울 수 있으며, 이는 모든 번역본에 적용된다. 피드백은 GitHub 저장소의 이슈로 받는다고 안내한다.

items.title: Wild version 0.11.0 released
items.content:

Lots of porting work has happened this release. The Wasm feature is now enabled by default, so Wild

can be used to link Wasm with the caveat that debug info isn't yet supported.

Support for GNU linker scripts is greatly enhanced. Wild now supports enough of the linker script

syntax that it can link Linux kernel modules and is close to being able to link the Linux kernel

The Mac port has made significant progress. The feature isn't yet to the point where we're prepared

to enable it by default, but Wild is able to link itself on Mac and at least one of the maintainers

is now using Wild as their default linker for Rust on Mac.

We've also fixed some performance issues that were affecting various filesystems and made a few

general performance improvements. We also got a bit slower due to implementing proper ELF COMDAT

We now cap the number of threads to at most 32 unless overridden by --threads. This avoids bad

performance that occurs with larger numbers of threads due to contention on a Linux per-inode mutex.

Our benchmarks have been expanded to include a wider range of scenarios such as different

filesystems and whether the output file already exists.

GNU 링커 스크립트 지원이 크게 강화되어 이제 Linux 커널 모듈을 링크할 수 있고, Linux 커널 전체 링크에도 가까워졌다. 맥 포트는 큰 진전을 이뤘다. 아직 기본값으로 켤 단계는 아니지만 Wild는 자기 자신을 맥에서 링크할 수 있으며, 메인테이너 중 한 명은 맥에서 Rust 기본 링커로 Wild를 쓰고 있다. 파일시스템별 성능 문제를 고쳤고 전반적인 성능도 개선했다. 다만 ELF COMDAT을 제대로 구현하면서 속도가 다소 느려졌다. 스레드는 --threads로 따로 지정하지 않으면 최대 32개로 제한된다. Linux inode별 뮤텍스 경합으로 스레드가 많을 때 성능이 나빠지는 문제를 피하기 위해서다. 벤치마크는 다양한 파일시스템 등 더 많은 시나리오를 포함하도록 확장됐다.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Physicists trap a single antimatter particle for a month
items.content:
Physicists trap a single antimatter particle for a month

For the first time, scientists can make quantum measurements on a positron particle

By Clara Moskowitz edited by Lee Billings

You can’t hold antimatter in your hand or even in a regular laboratory apparatus. As soon as antimatter meets matter , the two tend to annihilate each other. This makes studying antimatter tricky. But now physicists have managed to trap a single subatomic particle of the stuff for months at a time in a way that allows them to study its quantum states.

Further investigations using the trap might reveal the secret of why the world around us is made of matter and not antimatter , when things could have presumably gone either way.

Every normal particle of matter has an antimatter counterpart with equal mass but opposite charge. To build their trap, physicists started with atoms of sodium 22, a radioactive isotope with a half-life of about two and a half years. When one of these atoms decays, it emits a positron—the antimatter counterpart of the electron.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

“The big challenge is to persuade these positrons to slow down and then capture them,” says Gerald Gabrielse, a physicist at Northwestern University, who oversaw the project. The team reported its achievement on Wednesday in Physical Review Letters .

Gerald Gabrielse (top right) and his team in the lab where they trapped a positron particle for a month.

The first step is to send the positrons through the crystal lattice of a sliver of cold tungsten. As the particles go pinballing through the material, they slow down and lose energy. “Every time they bang into something, there’s a chance of annihilation, but it doesn’t always happen,” Gabrielse says. “If they make it to the end, they get popped out.”

Next, the physicists steer the positrons along a channel using electromagnetic fields. Eventually the particles end up in a vacuum, just three tenths of a degree Celsius above absolute zero, trapped by an electric field on top and bottom and a magnetic field on the sides. “If you want to hold on to antimatter, you have to hold it in a container without walls,” Gabrielse says.

This method allowed the researchers to isolate and study a solitary, lone positron for a month—and could let them do so indefinitely.

The researchers intend to use their trap to make precise measurements of the positron’s magnetic moment—basically the strength and orientation of its magnetic field. To do this, they must determine two things: the energy needed to flip the direction of the positron’s spin and the energy needed to make it jump from its ground state to its first excited state.

Using a similar trap setup, Gabrielse and his team have already measured the magnetic moment of an electron to a precision of one part in 10 trillion. Taking the equivalent measurement for a positron will allow them to make a crucial comparison. “We’re looking to see if they have an exactly opposite magnetic moment,” Gabrielse says. That’s the prediction of the Standard Model of particle physics. If the two have different values, however, this could help explain why our universe is made of matter instead of antimatter.

Just after the Big Bang, scientists think there were roughly equal amounts of the two. Most of the matter and antimatter must have annihilated, but a small excess of matter was somehow left over to seed the stars and planets we see. The magnetic moment measurement is just one of many realms where physicists are seeking differences between matter and antimatter to account for this profound discrepancy.

items.title: Be Aware of What's in Your Logs
items.content:
There is something I wish more people understood about bug reports, diagnostic information, and the apparently innocent act of attaching a log file to a support request, and it is this: your logs may contain things you really, really do not want anyone else reading.

I'm writing this because of a bug report I received recently, which came with a log file containing information I did not need to see, did not ask to see, and would have been perfectly happy going the rest of my life without ever seeing. I'm not going to identify the person who sent it, describe what was in it, or otherwise turn a perfectly understandable mistake into a public spectacle, because doing that to someone who was trying to help me fix my own software would be a spectacularly shitty thing to do. But the incident highlights something worth talking about, because I suspect an awful lot of people have absolutely no idea what they're handing over when they tick that little box labelled "Send logs," and the software they're using is rarely in any hurry to tell them.

A Log File Is Not Necessarily Just a Log File

When most people think of logs, they imagine a wall of boring technical gibberish: timestamps, error messages, stack traces, the occasional complaint about a missing file or something failing to initialise. Logs do contain those things. They can also contain an astonishing amount of information about what you were actually doing when the problem occurred, and depending on the application, its logging configuration, and the nature of the problem, that might include:

Usernames, email addresses, and account identifiers.

File paths containing your real name or other identifying details.

URLs, including query parameters and authentication tokens.

Information about other applications and services.

Internal application state that was never meant for public consumption.

Some applications log very little. Others log absolutely fucking everything, particularly once debugging is switched on, and you generally cannot tell which kind you're dealing with from the size of the file or the name of the feature. A file called debug.log sounds harmless enough, and that tells you precisely nothing about whether it is.

A log is a record of whatever an application considered relevant at a particular moment, and what an application considers relevant and what you consider private are two entirely different things. The computer has no idea that the conversation you were having was personal, that the document you had open was confidential, or that the text on your screen was something you'd rather not share with a stranger on the internet. It knows that something happened and that somebody told it to write that something down, so it did.

"Logs Can Contain Text Displayed on Screen"

I work on a screen reader, and like all software it occasionally misbehaves, which means I depend on people telling me when it does. The problem report form includes an option to send logs. That option is off by default, and when you get to it, the form warns you that logs can contain text displayed on screen. That warning is not decoration, and it's not there to cover my arse; it's there because I want people to understand what they might be about to send me.

A screen reader is in a particularly awkward position when it comes to privacy, because its entire job is to take whatever other applications put in front of you and make it accessible, which means it can encounter practically anything: your email, your private messages, your bank account, your medical records, your work documents, whatever happens to be on the screen at the time. When something goes wrong, diagnostic logging may well capture some of that, not because I'm secretly interested in what you get up to on your phone, but because the text a screen reader encountered is often directly relevant to why it behaved incorrectly. items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. items.title: Proton hosts map of 300,000 Flock devices amid legal threats
items.content:
Proton hosts map of 300,000 Flock devices amid legal threats

October 23, 2026 By Alex Lekander — Leave a Comment

Proton is hosting a public map showing more than 300,000 Flock surveillance devices across the United States, preserving access to a research project whose creator faces legal threats and intimidation.

The map draws on an inventory obtained by cybersecurity researcher Joshua Michael from Flock’s own systems. According to Proton, it includes more than 170,000 cameras and over 130,000 other devices.

In November 2025, Michael discovered that an access token could be obtained without logging in and used to retrieve device-location information. He reported the exposure to Flock and archived the inventory in December. His website dates the release of his formal research paper and surveillance map to September 23, 2026.

Proton, the Swiss company behind Proton Mail and Proton VPN , is offering another way to inspect Flock Safety’s footprint, whose automated license plate readers are used by police and private customers. The systems record passing vehicles regardless of whether their drivers are suspected of an offense, creating searchable records of plates, locations, and timestamps. Vehicle characteristics can also help identify cars without a readable plate.

Unlike crowdsourced projects such as DeFlock, Michael’s inventory comes from company records rather than sightings submitted by volunteers. However, Proton warns that the map reflects a December 2025 snapshot: subsequent installations and removals will not appear.

The dispute extends beyond the original security disclosure. In a September 25 update, Michael said Flock had sent him a cease-and-desist letter threatening litigation and told customers it had notified law enforcement.

In that notice, Flock said it had investigated the exposed token, closed the access path, and initially found no evidence of unauthorized access. Following further investigation in September, it identified anomalous activity involving the token but said its forensic review found no impact on customer data. Michael argues that the initial finding illustrates shortcomings in the company’s ability to detect access.

Earlier this week, 404 Media reported that California’s Orange County Intelligence Assessment Center had circulated a bulletin warning police about people attending city council meetings to oppose the surveillance technology.

Although it acknowledged that no specific, credible threats had been identified, the July bulletin urged officers to watch for suspicious behavior, including unusual questions and loitering. It also listed media attendance, livestreaming, and emotional exchanges among potential public safety concerns, bringing ordinary civic participation into a police threat-assessment framework. The center said its reporting supported safety planning and recognized constitutional protections for speech and assembly.

For residents, the map offers a starting point for asking local authorities where cameras operate, how long they retain vehicle records, which agencies can access them, and how they audit searches. Its age and coverage limitations mean it should be treated as a historical inventory rather than a complete picture of surveillance on today’s roads.

items.title: Node2Shell evolves to HTTP2Shell, blast radius affects many HTTP libs and apps
items.content:
Brotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It’s a way to make data smaller for storage or sending over the internet. Software then unpacks it to recover the original data. It’s widely used for HTTP compression to compress web content such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in the Google Brotli decoder affecting versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms. This is the same Brotli decoder flaw behind Node2Shell announced a couple days ago. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt memory, leak sensitive data, crash the process, or potentially execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical), and Node.js is affected through its bundled Brotli library.

A bug makes the Brotli decoder keep accepting more bytes when it should reject the data. Those bytes can overflow a small working buffer and damage the program’s memory. An attacker can use that damage to control what runs, such as their own code.

OpenAI found this in February reported it as unauthenticated remote code execution that works in both directions, so a malicious client can take over an unpatched server and a malicious server can take over an unpatched client that accepts compressed responses.

The root cause was fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn't recognized as a security issue at the time and no release shipped with the fix until now. That means every project that bundles Brotli has to ship its own update.

‍ You’re exposed if any environment has Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x installed, since HTTP clients such as requests, httpx, and aiohttp load these packages automatically when they’re present. Upgrade to Brotli 1.2.1 or brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 and rebuild any container images that bundle them. As of October 23, advisory databases don’t map the CVE to either PyPI package, so pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety won’t flag vulnerable versions yet.

‍ You can see what we’ve tracked here in Aikido Intel.

As for unaffected software, Apache’s standard mod_brotli does not decode Brotli

For CVE-2026-111497, update the affected runtime or Brotli library:

Update dependency locks, rebuild affected applications and container images, redeploy, and restart services. Verify that running workloads use the patched components.

These workarounds reduce exposure while you prepare the upgrade:

Changing Accept-Encoding alone is insufficient: a malicious server can send a Brotli response regardless of what the client advertises, and urllib3 selects its decoder from the response’s Content-Encoding header.

Keep these controls in place until affected components are patched and verified. Review coverage as vendors confirm additional affected components or attack paths.

Aikido flags vulnerable versions of Brotli and brotlicffi in your repositories, container images , and dependencies, including when they arrive as transitive dependencies. Your dashboard shows which services still run a vulnerable version, so you can upgrade the ones that call outside servers or accept compressed request bodies first.

Once you've upgraded, Aikido checks if the finding is gone.

Brotli is a widely used compression library from Google. On Wednesday, October 22nd NodeJS disclosed CVE-2026-111497, dubbed “node2shell,” wherein a Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data can be made to leak memory or run arbitrary code. Users were exposed if their app or a library decompresses bad Brotli data (e.g. the built-in fetch(), body-parser).

The next day, Python released a security update that patches the same flaw; Python packages were also vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497. Brotli flaw may affect even more languages and service applications, given how widely integrated the library is downstream. It turns out OpenAI had found this back in February.

items.summary_ko: C/C++에서 정의되지 않은 동작(UB)이 실제로 어떤 결과를 낳는지 어셈블리 예시로 보여주는 글이다. 일부 사람들은 UB가 문제없다고 주장하지만, 널 포인터 역참조 같은 코드는 컴파일러가 예상치 못한 기계어를 생성할 수 있다. 본문은 `std::unreachable()`을 `int* ptr = nullptr; *ptr = 99;`로 바꾸면 생성되는 코드에서 99가 아닌 0이 주소 0에 기록된 뒤 잘못된 명령으로 프로그램이 종료되는 과정을 보여준다.
items.content_ko: 본문은 메모리 매핑 장치를 제어하는 가상의 코드를 예로 든다. `std::unreachable()`은 해당 지점에서 정의되지 않은 동작을 일으킨다고 정의되어 있다. 이 경우 컴파일러는 `device_command`에 42를 쓰는 어셈블리를 생성하고, 이후 명령은 실행된다고 설명한다. 널 포인터 역참조 예시도 다룬다. 사람들은 주소 0에 접근하면 보통 세그먼트 폴트가 난다고 생각하지만, 컴파일된 결과는 다르다. 주소 0에 0이 먼저 기록되고, 이후 잘못된 명령으로 프로그램이 중단된다. 99는 생성된 프로그램에 나타나지 않지만, 널 포인터 쓰기는 실제로 남는다. 저자는 이것이 디버거의 오류 메시지를 개선하기 위한 것일 수 있다고 추측한다. 마지막에는 생성된 어셈블리 예시가 몇 개 더 제시된다.

items.title: Behind the Scenes, Meta’s Board Is Battling With Mark Zuckerberg Over His Out-of-Control AI Spending: The directors have had enough.
items.content:
Meta’s stocks have taken a serious beating lately, with its price shedding more than 13 percent over the past month. That fact isn’t likely to ease pressure in the trillion-dollar megacorp’s board room, as tensions between CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his board of directors reach a boiling point.

As the Wall Street Journal phrased it in new reporting, the conflict between Zuckerberg and his board have amounted to a “war over power and money.” Over the past few months, the paper reports, Zuckerberg has demanded a massive stock-heavy pay raise from Meta’s directorate, forcing an impasse so fraught that numerous board members have threatened to resign if the CEO doesn’t back down.

According to documents viewed by the WSJ , a negotiation team made up of three members of the board began preparing a contingency plan in early September, to use in the event that Zuckerberg refused to back down from his compensation demands. That standby plan reportedly included “resignation from the board” by the negotiation team as a last resort.

Though the squabble is playing out over Zuckerberg’s salary, the source of the conflict traces back to the CEO’s rampant spending on AI .

Per the WSJ , the whole remuneration debate was triggered by Meta’s out-of-control AI spending, which dragged the corporation into a negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion in the third quarter of 2026 — the first time the company has fallen into the red since 2012.

“More spending, negative free cash flow, not enough revenue being generated from the spend [is] concerning investors that this is just sort of a bit of a money pit,” as senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth Robert Pavlik told Reuters in an interview.

In an October 2025 investor meeting, Zuckerberg reportedly said his aggressive gamble on the AI-front was a necessary risk for Meta, despite simultaneously acknowledging that the hyperscale approach to AI had created a dangerous financial bubble.

“I think it’s the right strategy to aggressively front-load building capacity so that way we’re prepared for the most optimistic cases,” Zuckerberg told stockholders in 2025.

With Meta’s AI products failing security testing and automation implementation — to say nothing of the ongoing Muse safety debacle — it seems Zuckerberg’s AI ambitions are finally hitting the brick wall of financial reality.

items.title: Balloting has completed for C++26. Unfortunately it was Disapproved
items.content:
P-Members voting: 12 in favor out of 20 = 60 % (requirement >= 66.66%)

(P-Members having abstained are not counted in this vote.)

Member bodies voting: 9 negative votes out of 22 = 41 % (requirement <= 25%)

Sort of a sad day for the C++ community. Hopefully we can heal and move on from this in a productive manner.

There were 12 countries that abstained. In several cases because they could not reach to a common position. That is another signal of a contested draft.

Please, note that before C++26 all other standards passed unanimously.

Why should this be a sad day for the C++ community? Taking into account the number of P-members who abstained due to a lack of consensus, which makes the NO vote even more significant, sinking such a flawed contracts proposal is a good sign of a healthy, engaged, and competent community at the national body level.

That some people were willing to put the entire C++26 standard at risk to push through such a controversial and deeply flawed proposal is, of course, concerning. Fortunately, the national bodies recognized the problem before it was too late.

And perhaps it is also a clear signal that WG21's 'experts in the room' voting approach needs to be reconsidered.

I assume this was not a complete surprise and that those who voted against it had voiced opposition or at least reservations previously? Is the most promising path forward to reduce the scope and try again? Or were there things excluded that people really wanted?

Such is the life of standards. Anything particular?

It is hard to heal after the decades of the same social issues reappearing. What lessons should we learn to be able to move on in a productive manner?

12 in favor out of 20 who did not abstain gets 8 voting against, but then we have 9 negative votes out of 22? Not that it matters terribly since it doesn't seem very close.

So sad to hear this, but indeed, let's learn from this, and regroup and move on.

items.title: I don't understand quantum physics (2018)
Emacs finally folds to my liking
items.content:
I’ve been slowly turning my Emacs config into something I actually enjoy using, not just something that works, and folding was the last place where that wasn’t true.

Every mode had its own idea of what folding is: treesit-fold in Tree-sitter modes, Hideshow in the Lisp-ish ones, Outline in everything that resembles text, Org with its own invisible text that no one else’s commands can undo.

So every buffer had different keys, a different look, and worst of all different performance characteristics. Folding a big file sometimes felt like holding my breath.

I’m running Emacs 32.0.50 from master (built from source, as one does), and it’s finally one system.

kirigami doesn’t fold anything itself. It dispatches : it keeps a list of folding engines, checks which one is actually active in the buffer, and forwards to it. Tree-sitter, Hideshow, Outline, Org, Vdiff — all behind one interface.

So on top of it I put one set of keys, the same in a Kotlin buffer, YAML, a Scheme or ELisp buffer and an Org file:

That sounds small. It is not small. The number of times a day I used to think “wait, what does TAB do in this mode again” is now zero, and the muscle memory transfers across an entire polyglot config.

One wrinkle worth mentioning: kirigami answers with the first engine in its list whose mode is on, and outline-minor-mode is on in nearly every buffer I have. In the buffers where I deliberately turned on Hideshow — Scheme, for instance — that choice has to win, otherwise C-c v c folds “headings” a Scheme file doesn’t have. So I reorder kirigami-fold-list to put Hideshow first instead of rewriting it; engines kirigami adds later still get used wherever Hideshow is off.

Most of my programming buffers are *-ts-mode , so treesit-fold does the work there — bash, C, C++, CMake, CSS, Dockerfile, Elixir, Go, HTML, Java, JS/TS/TSX, JSON, Kotlin, Lua, Nix, PHP, Python, Ruby, Rust, Scala, TOML, YAML. Line counts are shown inline, which I find genuinely useful when deciding whether to open a fold.

The indicators took the most fiddling. treesit-fold-indicators draws a block’s guide with a bitmap 23 rows tall, centered in the line beside it. A line in my config is 29 pixels — the font’s 23 plus six of line-spacing — so every row of the guide was a 23-pixel dash with three pixels of nothing above and below it. A folded block looked like a dotted line running down the fringe. Not subtle, just wrong.

There’s no setting for that, so I replaced the bitmaps: a single-row bitmap that define-fringe-bitmap repeats down however tall the line is (no spacing can introduce a gap), plus a +=/ -= box and an end-elbow cut to the exact height of a line, so the guide runs from the marker into the row below and turns toward the text where the block ends. It’s an advice on the function that builds the string for each line. It looks like a bracket now, not a perforation.

And the colour: the indicators inherited shadow , which most themes make as bright as a comment. Fine for one marker on one line, wrong for a marker on every line of a block — the grey became a rule drawn through the code. They’re now shadow blended 50% toward the theme’s background, recomputed on every theme and scale change, so it fades correctly on light themes too and no theme needs a special entry.

Not everything has a grammar, and I’m not going to pretend otherwise:

Hideshow’s own fringe indicators ( hs-show-indicators + hs-indicator-type 'fringe ) are on in all of these, so it doesn’t feel like a downgrade from the Tree-sitter buffers.

The rule I enforce per buffer is exactly one set of indicators : Tree-sitter buffers get treesit-fold and Hideshow is turned off; Hideshow buffers get Hideshow and Outline’s clickable buttons are turned off so the two don’t double up; outline-only buffers (Markdown, diff) keep the buttons. Nobody ends up with two markers per block.

Org folds with text properties, not overlays, so neither Tree-sitter nor Hideshow nor Outline’s buttons can draw a marker…

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

MapQuest now showing surveillance camera locations across Canada, U.S.
items.content:
MapQuest users in Canada and the U.S. can now see where some surveillance cameras have been set up in their communities.

The company introduced a "surveillance layer" earlier this week that uses animated eyes to mark where automated licence plate readers, or ALPRs, have been set up by police or others.

"We knew that there were a ton of cameras in use and documented in the U.S. and Canada," MapQuest general manager Doug Berger told CBC News. "You would never know unless they were pointed out to you."

The U.S.-based online mapping service recently went viral, three decades after it launched, after refusing to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" following U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order demanding the switch. (Apple and Google changed the lake's name for U.S. users.)

Some three million people in the U.S. and Canada downloaded the app following the move, according to Berger.

"The coolest part of that experience was people were — and still today people are — telling us exactly what they want," he said.

One of the requests was to be able to see surveillance camera locations, he said.

MapQuest's Doug Berger on the app's new found popularity after standing strong on Lake Ontario name

Police have maintained that ALPRs are an effective tool for identifying criminals, stolen vehicles and missing persons, and that most data is quickly deleted.

The data is "used solely for law enforcement purposes by authorized personnel only," according to the Toronto Police Service, for example.

But a recent CBC News report found that the growing popularity of ALPRs, especially in the U.S., has raised privacy concerns.

"There are concerns of misuse," the Canadian Civil Liberties Association's Tamir Israel said in August. "It's been documented in the U.S. that these cameras have been misused by police officers to follow ex-partners around and that kind of thing."

The map markings include cameras set up by Flock, the private company whose ALPRs have stirred controversy and vandalism across the U.S. Other companies behind public cameras include Genetec, PlateSmart, Neology and Verkada.

Berger says highlighting ALPR locations is about transparency.

"We're not taking a political stance against the efficacy of them or anything, but we are bringing forth the visibility of them for people using the MapQuest app in an effort to be transparent," he said.

Camera locations are indicated on the MapQuest mobile app, which is only available to Canadian and U.S. users. The locations are based on open crowd-sourced data from OpenStreetMap.

The locations of licence plate readers like this one in Cornwall, P.E.I., are crowd-sourced data from OpenStreetMap. (CBC)

In the app, an icon in the map's lower right corner symbolizes the layers, with one square on top of another. By tapping the icon, a user can select the "surveillance" feature. Within seconds, eyes that shift side to side pop on the screen.

"Our team had a lot of fun with that," Berger said, adding that the eye fit with a few additional Halloween-themed launches.

"The moving eye was spooky and fit nicely with the theme of the Halloween release," Berger said. "At the moment, we don't see a reason to change it. It gives a good strong visual to go along with the fact that there are cameras."

As for the sheer number of eyes that pop up in various neighbourhoods: "It's pretty crazy," Berger said.
