items.title: How close can pure functional programming get to C?
items.content:
In Why Lean is Faster Than Rust , the author shares an impressive result: a DEFLATE compression library written in Lean 4 , a functional programming language and proof assistant, outperforming an equivalent Rust package that crates.io says has been downloaded over a billion times. From the article:

lean-zip beats every single compression level miniz_oxide provides, i.e. we're capable of providing the same compression at higher throughput. At its fastest setting we're 15% quicker and the output is 8.8% smaller.

However, the article also notes that while they managed to surpass Rust's miniz_oxide , they were no match for the end boss of DEFLATE performance: libdeflate , written in C.

lean-zip is certainly not the best here: libdeflate unsurprisingly blows it out of the water (unsurprisingly because this is a very carefully tuned implementation using architecture-specific SIMD, that we can't touch in Lean).

Enter Roc , a functional programming language (but not a theorem prover) with an explicit focus on runtime performance.

Roc's tagline is "Fast, Friendly, Functional," and Fast comes first because both running fast and compiling fast have always been central goals. Roc is not a mature language (it's still weeks away from its first numbered release, 0.1.0), and its nascent package ecosystem has had almost no optimization work done on it. Still, between its language design, longstanding optimizations , and brand-new compiler implementation , I figured Roc already had enough of a foundation in place to take on the champ: libdeflate.

So I spent a bunch of time grinding through performance optimizations on roc-deflate , a package Niclas Ahden wrote (and uses in paid production work ) for DEFLATE compression. I didn't expect to beat libdeflate's performance across the board, but I wanted to see how close it could get on the non-streaming APIs (as roc-deflate hasn't implemented streaming yet), using the classic Silesia corpus for benchmarking and verifying that it produced identical outputs.

Here's where the benchmarks stand today, running on the 2021 M1 MacBook Pro where I did all the optimization work, as well as on an AMD Ryzen 9 3900X Ubuntu machine for an x64 comparison.

roc-deflate ran these 144 benchmarks slower on average than libdeflate, in the median case 8.9% slower on the Ryzen 3900X, and 2.6% on the M1 MacBook Pro.

So while we didn't outperform the champ on average, a median slowdown percentage in the single digits compared to such a carefully-tuned SIMD-powered C library is wild. It's frankly not a result I knew was achievable going in, since Roc is a functional language with automatic memory management racing against code that doesn't have to do bounds checks. (Bounds checks have a cost, but then again, the last time a skipped bounds check in C compression code led to a major Remote Code Execution vulnerability was yesterday .)

The graph shows more detail than just the median gap. On the worst-case inputs, roc-deflate was 18% slower than libdeflate, but on the best-case inputs, roc-deflate was slightly over 18% faster! That's not because Roc has some magical optimization that C can't access; it's just that the two implementations are different, and although on average roc-deflate is slower, for certain inputs it happens to be faster. So while it's possible to get a speedup by switching from libdeflate to roc-deflate, you shouldn't expect it on average.

To be clear, C's performance ceiling is higher than Roc's. For any input where roc-deflate currently outperforms libdeflate, C code can close that gap. The reverse is not true; Roc code is memory-safe, does automatic reference counting, checks bounds, and supports no Rust-style unsafe to opt out of any of that. These properties give Roc code stronger safety guarantees than code written in C, Zig, Rust, and other languages that allow full access to the hardware—and the price it pays for those guarantees is a lower performance ceiling.

items.title: How to run a city builder on 16 MHz
items.content:
Do you feel spoiled by modern hardware? I know I do. Even the cheapest CPUs have at least 4 cores nowadays, running billions of operations per second. The idea that you could run any software on less than a GHz almost seems like fiction. Yet, there was a time when whole games ran at hardware a thousand times less powerful than that.

When thinking about impressive technical achievements in retro games, most people will first point to graphical milestones set by action games like Doom or Quake. Rightfully so, but at least I am personally far more impressed by the early examples of the city builder genre. Simulating whole economies on a large scale with a fraction of today’s power seems impossible if modern builder games even struggle on modern machines.

Of course this didn’t stop developers in the past to develop and run city builder games on significantly weaker hardware. The original SimCity for example lists Intel’s 386SX as the CPU in it’s system requirements. A CPU which at the time of it’s launch ran at magnificent 16 MHz.

(Note: an earlier version of this text mistakenly assumed that it ran on 12.5 MHz, which was the clock rate of base version of CPU, not the SX version. Whoops.)

The idea of running a full game, especially one in the traditionally CPU-heavy genre of city builders? Pure magic from a modern point point of view.

So, why could Maxis run a full city simulation on this ancient hardware, when nowadays even simple idle games require multiple gigahertz of CPU power?

Of course there are a lot of reason for this, most of them external (OS ecosystem etc.) but this doesn’t mean that there are no clever optimizations done in the game code itself. Luckily, this source code was made public and released under the GPL license in 2008, under the name Micropolis . Don’t be confused by the name, this is still the code of the original name, but since only the code was made open source, not the trademark, it has to be called differently. But even under a different name, this is a precious resource, since we can exactly see how the game managed to run so well.

As is often the case when analyzing software performance, we can ignore 90 percent of the code. Our focus is on the core of the city simulation, the components that update systems such as traffic, fire, power, and crime.

And there is indeed one single function responsible for doing all of this: The Simulate() function in s_sim.c

As the comment implies, this function is called every frame and the function itself then calls the update functions of the various game systems, like CrimeScan(), FireAnalysis(), CollectTax etc.

The catch is that calling all those functions every frame would overwhelm our poor 1989 CPU. The solution: Not calling every function every frame.

Yep, SimCity just skips most of the simulation. Did you see the mod16 parameter of the Simulate function? Where you would normally expect a deltaTime? This number loops through the numbers 0 to 15 (you probably knew this already because of the name, didn’t you?), and is then used to decided which part of the simulation is run in this specific frame. (Note: This is not the exact source, I removed some stuff to make it clearer for the explanation, but it’s veery close) .

So, obviously this makes the Simulation much faster to calculate, but how does this affect the gameplay? Well in case of SimCity, I would say barely. On average the simulation of an aspect takes 8 frames to react to the player’s action, 15 frames in the worst case. As an input lag for a shooter this would be obviously a disaster, but for the simulation of a city? I’d argue it might actually feel better than an instant reaction.

So far this optimization seems very specific for one kind of type of game, but actually it is the starting point for a lot of optimizations.

items.title: Man Hires Swarm of AI Agents to Go on Epic Hacking Spree Against Major Companies
items.content:
A cybercriminal used AI agents to commit a string of attacks against more than 100 different companies — an alarming incident that shows how autonomous agents with advanced AI hacking capabilities have exponentially raised the threat that a single human hacker can pose.

As Reuters first reported , a threat researcher at the cybersecurity company NorForge discovered that a Chinese-speaking hacker had used autonomous agents to carry out the mass hacking spree, which impacted global companies including John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins, among dozens of others.

The hacker isn’t alone. According to Snorre Fagerland, the researcher who discovered the Deere and SharkNinja hacker, the cybercriminal is one of several malicious actors who have abused an open source AI tool called Cairn to send swarms of agents on autonomous hacking sprees.

“It’s ​a new world now,” Fagerland, who detailed his findings in a report , told Reuters.

One of the Cairn-assisted hackers who Fagerland observed was able to make away with sensitive credit card information, according to the report.

The Chinese speaking hacker was the most aggressive, per Reuters . They deployed AI systems against over 1,200 US, Canadian, Australian and Japanese ​e-commerce sites, with successful breaches occurring after the AI agents attacked different companies for about 23 hours. Each successful hack reportedly cost about $50 in tokens, and according to Fagerland, the techniques used by the agents were sophisticated.

“It’s ⁠not straightforward to come up with solutions like that,” Fagerland told Reuters . “It’s not script kiddie stuff.”

Deere told Reuters that it had taken “necessary remediation actions” in response to the breach, and said that there was “no indication that ​sensitive information was accessed.” SharkNinja told the outlet that that the hacker had accessed a site that didn’t contain sensitive data, while Cummins relayed that it was “investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of our third-party vendors.”

The report is the latest to shed light on the global cybersecurity crisis wrought by advanced AI and its ability to find and exploit existing vulnerabilities in the code maintaining the world’s digital infrastructure. If the web is made of sticks and glue, AI has handed bad actors bundles of cheap TNT to plant across the internet. And while AI agents are helping normies send emails, book dinner reservations, and manage calendars, they’re also helping cybercriminals set autonomous swarms of capable, always-on hackers loose on online world.

items.title: Updated Google privacy policy says your Gmail might be used for advertising
items.content:
Using Google’s products and services has always been fundamentally precarious—doing so gives the world’s largest advertising company a lot of juicy personal data. Google has long said it won’t use the sensitive data from products like Gmail, Drive, and Photos for ad personalization, but a change to the company’s privacy policy appears to dismantle that firewall.

On October 16, Google issued an update to its privacy policy , spotted by Android Authority . The ad personalization section used to include a clear limit on data from certain apps. “We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos,” the document said. Now, Google has updated it with the following language.

Updated language on when your sensitive data might inform ads.

Updated language on when your sensitive data might inform ads.

This equivocation opens the door to using data from apps like Gmail and Photos in ads when it’s shared with other Google services, and it just so happens Google has a mechanism for doing that, with Personal Intelligence. The company released Personal Intelligence in early 2026 , allowing users to hand data from multiple apps to Google AI products. The idea is that the added context from your existing data will lead to better AI answers, but it’s also proving to be a privacy minefield.

Personal Intelligence connects your data to the Gemini app but also to features like AI Mode search. While the Gemini app does not currently have ads, you may see sponsored content in AI search tools. Google’s changes to the privacy policy appear to acknowledge that data shared with AI search via Personal Intelligence could, therefore, contribute to ad personalization.

According to Google, this clarification still doesn’t mean ads are “based directly” on your personal data. Here’s the company’s full statement:

“Connecting your apps is entirely opt-in. Ads will continue to be relevant to things like your query, the context of the response and your interests. Ads will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or Photos library, and as always, sensitive information will not be used to tailor ads.”

Google’s statement is essentially a roundabout way of confirming that Workspace and Photos data may inform ads. If you interact with AI Mode while Personal Intelligence is enabled, there’s a chance that summaries and insights from your data will inform the answers you get. Because that same data is used for ad targeting, it’s accurate to say that your personal data is an element of ad targeting in AI search. The privacy policy now makes that clear.

A Google spokesperson tells Ars that its privacy clarification does not indicate a change in how it handles your data with respect to its advertising partners. It’s not scanning your entire inbox to enhance your advertising profile, and it’s not giving any of this data to third parties. But if you pipe personal data into an AI search tool, the ads it shows you could be based on that information.

The core of the problem is that Google wants its products and services to talk to each other. Google sees that wealth of data as a key strength of its AI efforts. Some apps like Gmail are still given protected status in Google’s data handling, but there are now more avenues for that data to get out. The more data you share across Google’s ecosystem, the greater the risk to your privacy.

We’ve seen a similar exception in the way Google uses your AI interactions for model training . While Google says it doesn’t use personal data for AI training, it does use your inputs and the model outputs for that purpose. With Gemini integrated with so many services and connected to them via Personal Intelligence, those outputs may very well contain elements of your personal information. Google has said it tries to filter that content from the user activity controls, therefore keeping it out of training sets. However, it doesn’t promise it will always be successful.

The glorious @xkcdRandom Zig builtin
items.content:
One of my favorite xkcd comics of all time is Random Number . The image depicts a C function that supposedly returns a random integer, but in reality always returns 4 . I was reminded of this wonderful comic a few days ago, due to a security incident where people accidentally used the number 4 (among others) instead of a properly generated sequence of random bytes. Satire has a tendency to become reality, I guess.

Since there is a clear demand among developers for the xkcd random number generator, I’m of the opinion that self-respecting languages should ship a built-in implementation. I’m here today to lead by example, as I unveil the glorious @xkcdRandom builtin for the Zig language. Can you guess what it does? Indeed, it returns the number 4 ! Now go found a multi-billion-dollar startup on top of this genius idea.

Why not? After completing the Ziglings exercises and brain-coding a toy minesweeper game , I felt like my grasp of the language was solid enough to attempt something more ambitious. I wanted to get my hands on production-grade Zig code, and play with it to see how the different pieces of the language fit together. Hacking on the Zig compiler sounded like the perfect idea!

A sane person might implement the xkcd RNG as a literal port of the original C code, which maps to the following Zig function:

There’s one very big drawback to this approach: it’s boring. Don’t get me wrong, I like boring and low-maintenance code as much as the next person… but this time my goal is to learn , not to produce . I actually want to jump through hoops and make things overly complicated! Builtins are perfect for this. They are, as the name suggests, built-in constructs in the Zig language. Adding one means I get to fork and modify the compiler. Yay!

The builtin source code is intertwined with the rest of the Zig compiler, so it’s not really possible to include it here. Feel free to inspect the diff if you are curious (it’s just 22 lines), or to clone my Zig fork and check out the 0.17.x-xkcd branch.

With these changes to the compiler, you can build programs like the one below. Isn’t that neat?

The Zig developers have clearly put effort into developer experience. You can build Zig with a single command: zig build --zig-lib=lib -Dno-lib -Ddev=x86_64-linux . The fresh build took roughly a minute to complete on my laptop, which in my book is quite good for a compiler. Subsequent builds were faster.

As for the coding work itself, an LLM pointed me to the file where builtins were defined, and I took over from there: modifying things, checking for compile errors, fixing them, and so on. The code was easy to navigate, thanks to its clear structure and the Zig language server’s help. I was done way faster than I expected! Maybe I should find a real compiler issue to tackle next.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.content_ko: 보안 연구자 Nightmare-Eclipse가 공개한 YellowKey 제로데이 취약점은 물리적 접근만으로 Windows 11 기본 BitLocker 보호를 우회할 수 있다. BitLocker는 Microsoft가 제공하는 전체 볼륨 암호화 기술로, 신뢰할 수 있는 플랫폼 모듈(TPM)에 저장된 복호화 키 없이는 디스크 접근이 불가능하도록 설계되었다. 많은 조직과 정부 계약업체에서 필수 보호 기술로 사용 중이다. YellowKey 익스플로잇의 핵심은 커스텀으로 만들어진 FsTx 폴더 사용으로, fstx.dll과 관련된 디렉터리는 Microsoft의 transactional NTFS 기술을 활용한다.

items.content_ko: 작성자는 파리의 Hexacon에서 공개한 일련의 데모를 소개하며 iPhone 해킹에 성공했다고 밝힙니다. 모든 내용은 적절한 시기에 공개될 예정입니다. 본문은 짧은 게시글 형식이며, 서드파티 앱과 iMessage를 언급하는 문장과 'APT는 Apple Persistent Threat의 약자'라는 설명이 있습니다. 기술적인 세부 내용은 포함되어 있지 않습니다.

items.title: Hugging Force: the Hub as a galaxy you can fly through
사생활침해 범죄가 의심 됩니다. 도움이 필요합니다
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다
